lessons.title: What the cold chain is and why it matters
lessons.html:
Fruit is alive

After fruit is picked, it is still alive. It keeps breathing (respiring), uses up its sugar and water, and slowly ripens and then goes soft and rots. Heat makes this happen much faster. Cold slows it down.

The cold chain is the whole chain of steps that keeps fruit cool from the orchard to the customer. South African fruit such as citrus, apples, pears, table grapes and stone fruit travels for weeks by ship to Europe, Asia and the Middle East. It only arrives in good condition if the cold chain is never broken.

The links in the chain

  1. Orchard: pick in the cool of the day and put bins in the shade.
  2. Transport to packhouse: move fruit quickly; cover loads.
  3. Pre-cooling: remove field heat quickly, for example with forced-air cooling.
  4. Packing: pack without delay; keep packed fruit out of the sun.
  5. Cold storage: store at the correct temperature for that fruit.
  6. Loading: load refrigerated trucks or containers quickly from a cold loading area.
  7. Port and ship: refrigerated (reefer) containers or ship holds keep the set temperature.
  8. Market: importer cold stores, distribution centres and shop fridges.

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link

If a pallet stands in the sun for two hours on a loading dock, the damage cannot be undone by cooling it later. The fruit may arrive soft, rotten, shrivelled or with shorter shelf life. The buyer can reject the whole consignment and the farmer loses money.

Different fruit, different temperatures

Each fruit kind, and sometimes each cultivar or market, has its own correct temperature and protocol. Some fruit can be damaged by too much cold (chilling injury). Always follow the temperature set in your packhouse's instructions or the export protocol; never guess.

lessons.title: Your role in keeping the chain unbroken
lessons.html:
Temperature control at work

Every worker in the packhouse and cold store has a part in the cold chain.

Good practice

  • Keep cold room doors closed. Open them only when needed and close them straight away. Use strip curtains if fitted.
  • Do not leave pallets or bins standing outside the cold room, on the dock or in the sun.
  • Stack pallets so that cold air can flow around them. Do not block the fans or air vents.
  • Follow the first in, first out rule so older fruit is shipped first, unless told otherwise.
  • Report broken doors, ice build-up, strange noises from the fridge plant or rising temperatures immediately.

Measuring temperature

Temperatures are checked with thermometers, probes and data loggers.

  • Air temperature is shown on the cold room display.
  • Pulp temperature is the temperature inside the fruit, measured with a clean probe pushed into the fruit. This is what really matters.
  • Data loggers or temperature recorders are often placed in pallets or containers to record the temperature throughout the journey.

Write readings on the record sheet with the date, time, room number and your name. If a reading is outside the allowed range, tell your supervisor at once.

Loading containers

Before loading, the reefer container must be pre-cooled to the set temperature, clean, and in working order. Load quickly, close doors, and record the container number, seal number and set temperature.

Safety in cold stores

  • Wear warm protective clothing.
  • Know where the inside door release and alarm are. Never allow anyone to be locked in.
  • Watch for forklifts and keep to walkways.
  • Floors can be slippery with ice or water.

Key points

  • Fruit is alive after picking, and heat speeds up its breakdown.
  • The cold chain keeps fruit cool from orchard to customer.
  • One broken link can ruin a consignment.
  • Keep doors closed, do not leave fruit in the sun, and allow air flow.
  • Check and record pulp and air temperatures; report problems immediately.
